newsitem.title: UK: Rhone launches bowel cancer drug in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Rhone launches bowel cancer drug in Europe.

text.p: Rhone-Poulenc Rorer launched its new bowel cancer drug Campto in Europe on Wednesday and said it helped stop the deadly cancer in more than half of patients who failed to respond to traditional drugs.

Campto, licensed by Rhone for sale in more than 100 countries from Yakult Honsha Co Ltd of Japan, is approved for second-line treatment of colorectal cancer in patients who have not responded to standard 5-fluorouracil treatment.

"Many patients with 5-FU resistant metastatic colorectal cencer may now be able to derive benefit from Campto," said David Cunningham, an oncologist at the Royal Marsden Hospital. "Until now there has been no licensed therapeutic option for those who have relapsed with 5-FU treatment."
He said patients in whom the drug worked gained weight and got pain relief.

Bowel cancer is the second most prevalent cancer in the western world and the incidence is rising. In Europe, about 160,000 people are diagnosed with bowel cancer every year and 95,000 will die from it. It is linked with a diet low in fibre and high in animal fat, excess calories and alcohol.
Campto (irinotecan hydrochloride trihydrate) was cleared by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration last summer for marketing in the United States by Pharmacia & Upjohn.

The first new cytotoxic drug treatment for bowel cancer in 40 years, it inhibits topoisomerase I, an enzyme involved in cell division. Scientists became interested because this property could make it kill tumour cells specifically.
Side-effects are the standard for cancer chemotherapy -- low white blood cell counts, nausea, diarrhoea and hair loss.

It is a semi-synthetic derivative of camptothecin, a plant alkaloid from the bark of the Asian tree Camptotheca acuminata. Its anti-tumour properties were discovered by accident but now most drugs companies have developed derivatives.
Bowel cancer drugs are potential big business for pharmaceutical companies.
Britain's Zeneca Group Plc recently launched Tomudex, a thymidylate synthase inhibitor, in Europe and is expected to file for FDA approval this year.
Zeneca says the first-line drug is equivalent to 5-FU without the side-effects.
